title: Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for fats, including saturated fatty acids, polyunsaturated fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids, trans fatty acids, and cholesterol
authors: EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products, Nutrition, and Allergies (NDA)
funder: European Food Safety Authority, on request from the European Commission (Question No EFSA-Q-2008-466).
result: Humans lack delta-12 and delta-15 desaturases, so linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential; n-6 and n-3 fatty acids are desaturated and elongated by the same enzymes. Adequate intake 4% of energy for linoleic acid and 0.5% for alpha-linolenic acid. Less than 1% of deuterated linoleic acid was converted to arachidonic acid; alpha-linolenic acid conversion about 8 to 12% to EPA and less than 1% to DHA; conversion of ALA decreases as dietary linoleic acid increases; amounts of n-3 LCPUFA formed depend on ALA intake, not on the n-3/n-6 ratio. Linoleic acid has a negative, dose-dependent relationship with LDL cholesterol. No specific values set for the n-3/n-6 ratio because data on clinical and biochemical endpoints in humans are insufficient to recommend a ratio independent of absolute intakes. No consistent evidence that n-6 PUFA intake has detrimental effects; no upper level set.
